source.title: Large Language Models for Test-Free Fault Localization
source.citation: Ai-Dan Z. H. Yang et al., 2023
source.authors: Ai-Dan Z. H. Yang; Claire Le Goues; Ruben Martins; Vincent J. Hellendoorn

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests the downstream-performance-with-scale version using fault-localization metrics rather than pretraining loss or the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper varies the size of the pretrained CodeGen model and reports fault-localization results. It does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, fit scaling laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its discussion of scaling laws and its citations to Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are not results from this study.
record.test_reason: In an RQ3 ablation, the paper swaps the frozen CodeGen backbone (350M, 6B, 16B) under its own fault-localization adapter and reports Top-N and AUC at each size. That is a downstream-performance-versus-scale result in a new setting (frozen-feature, line-level fault localization), so T3 fits better than T2. It fits no curve, reports no pretraining loss and makes no forecast. Hyperparameters also differ by size (Table 1: learning rates, model dimension), so size is not cleanly isolated.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that fault-localization performance scales consistently with backbone size and that CodeGen-16B gives the highest AUC on all studied datasets. They also conclude that the bidirectional adapter is essential. They add that performance rises with labeled dataset size.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream fault-localization evaluation, not a reproduction of language-model cross-entropy scaling experiments; it varies pretrained CodeGen size and measures fault-localization metrics.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling results concern LLMAO with its bidirectional adapter and vary the underlying CodeGen checkpoint size.

fits_no_version.finding: Across datasets, performance with CodeGen-16B is higher on the larger labeled datasets (Devign Top-5 60.3%, AUC 0.855; BugsInPy Top-5 15.2%, AUC 0.571). The comparison is confounded by language and defect domain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream fine-tuned task performance grows with the amount of labeled fine-tuning data.

record.peer_reviewed: 2024 IEEE/ACM 46th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE '24)
record.problems: The scale comparison uses only three pretrained model sizes and a downstream fault-localization task, not held-out pretraining loss. It does not fit a scale curve or report predictions for larger runs. Uncertainty is not reported for the size-comparison values themselves; the paper's Wilcoxon tests concern comparisons with prior techniques and ablations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Table 3 reports aggregate results across datasets without identifying a specific CodeGen size, so those figures cannot be assigned to a size-scaling condition. Baseline fault-localization comparisons that do not vary model size are also outside the tested scaling result.

untested.parts: Whether gains are predictable, i.e. follow a fitted function of scale or of pretraining loss. Forecasting larger models. Downstream tasks other than fault localization. Per-size results on BugsInPy and Devign are only plotted, not tabulated.
Not tested: no pretraining loss measured.
Not tested: no fits or extrapolation.
Not tested: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no power-law form in other regimes.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-size (350M, 6B, 16B) ROC/AUC on BugsInPy and Devign. The paper states the largest model has the highest AUC on all datasets, but gives numbers only for 16B (0.571, 0.855).
RQ4 says all three sizes were run on BugsInPy and Devign, but Table 3 reports only one configuration (it matches 16B for Defects4J). Per-size Top-N for these datasets is not given.

record.verdict_notes: The scale comparison is an ablation inside a tool paper. Per-size hyperparameters differ (Table 1 learning rates and dimensions), although the text claims a uniform dimension of 512, which is inconsistent. Only three sizes are tested, with no uncertainty for the size comparison; the Wilcoxon tests concern baselines and ablations. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as motivation and for the learning-rate schedule.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law forms across modalities or training regimes.

Tests fault-localization outcomes against pretrained model size, but not predictions from pretraining loss, quantitative forecasts from a fitted scale curve, or downstream tasks beyond the fault-localization settings studied.
No comparison of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or setups.

relationships.condition: LLMAO on Defects4J V1.2.0, Top-3, Top-5 and AUC, frozen CodeGen 350M to 6B to 16B
relationships.reason: Top-5 rises 126 to 160 to 183, Top-3 rises 106 to 115 to 149, and AUC rises 0.573 to 0.638 to 0.677, monotonic in size (r5, r6, r8, r9, r12, r13).
relationships.display_finding: Top-5 increased through 126, 160, and 183, Top-3 through 106, 115, and 149, and AUC through 0.573, 0.638, and 0.677.

relationships.reason: Top-1 gains are small: +3 faults per size step, about 0.7 percentage points, despite a 45x parameter increase overall (r4, r7). The step sizes are also uneven across metrics (e.g. Top-3 gains +9 then +34).
relationships.display_finding: Top-1 gained only three faults per size step, about 0.7 percentage points despite 45-fold overall parameter growth, while Top-3 gains were nine then 34 faults.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
